Draft:

I agree with the principal's decision that every student should take part in at least one extracurricular activity. Some students will grumble at first, and a few will say their afternoons are already full. But school is supposed to prepare us for more than tests, and a required activity gives every student a chance to learn things a classroom rarely teaches.

The strongest reason is that these activities build skills that grades do not measure. Think about the yearbook. To finish one book, a team of students has to plan page layouts, take and sort photographs, write captions, and meet a printer's deadline. If one person falls behind, the whole book is late. A student who spends a year on that team learns to manage time, to take feedback from an editor, and to depend on classmates and be depended on in return. Student council works the same way. A council member who helps organize a fall dance has to build a budget, persuade teachers to help, and handle complaints when the music is too loud. Those are the same abilities employers say they look for, and most students get little practice with them in a regular class schedule.

A second reason is that extracurriculars help students find where they belong. Every school has quiet students who walk in, sit through their classes, and leave without really knowing anyone. I have seen this happen. A boy in my grade barely spoke until he joined the cross-country team. He was not the fastest runner, but he was welcomed on long bus rides and at team dinners, and by spring he was cheering loudly for teammates he had never met the autumn before. Belonging to something makes a student want to come to school. Research on attendance and dropout rates often finds that students who are connected to a club or team are less likely to leave school early. If the rule gets even a few lonely students to find a group, it has already been worth it.

Some people object that a requirement takes away choice. They say students should join only what they truly care about, and that forced participation will lead to bored, careless members. That concern is fair, but the decision leaves plenty of room for choice. The principal did not say everyone must play football. The list includes sports, yearbook, and student council, and a school can add chess club, drama, band, a recycling committee, or a robotics team. A student who dislikes competition can paint sets for the spring play. A student who loves computers can run the school website. The rule only says that everyone must pick something. Choosing among many options is still a real choice, and it pushes students to try something they might never have considered otherwise. Many of us do not know what we enjoy until we have tried it.

Another worry is time. Some students have jobs, care for younger siblings, or have heavy homework loads. A good policy should account for this. The school can offer activities that meet during lunch or only once a week, and it can let a part-time job or family duties count in special cases. Flexibility makes the rule fair without defeating its purpose. A student who is busy still benefits from one small commitment, because it creates a routine that includes other people and something to look forward to.

Finally, the habit matters beyond high school. Adults who volunteer, coach a youth team, or serve on a neighborhood board usually began by joining things when they were young. Learning early that you can contribute to a group, and that the group is better for it, prepares students to be active citizens. A school that asks all of its students to practice that habit is investing in the community they will someday lead.

For these reasons, I support the principal's decision. Extracurricular activities teach teamwork and responsibility, they help isolated students connect, and they give everyone a chance to discover a talent. With sensible options and some flexibility, requiring one activity per student is a small demand with a large reward.
